Somewhere in your truck right now, a connected system is quietly recording how it is driven, how hard it works, where it goes, and how healthy its engine is, and that stream of data is no longer just a maintenance convenience, it is becoming one of the most important numbers in your business, because at a recent candid session with Daimler Truck leadership, a reporter cut straight to the point and asked whether all that telematics information is effectively his new credit score, and the answer from the people who finance and insure trucks was close to yes.
That exchange deserves attention from every carrier, because it marks a real shift. The information your equipment generates is increasingly shaping what you pay for insurance, how quickly you get financed, how your warranty claims are handled, and even how a lender sizes up the risk of doing business with you. Here is what Daimler’s leaders said about how that data is already being used, and what it means for an operator trying to protect both the bottom line and a little privacy.
From Maintenance Tool To Risk Engine
Telematics started as a maintenance and tracking tool. You could see where your trucks were and get a heads-up when something needed attention. What has changed is that the same data is now feeding decisions that used to be made with paperwork, gut feel, and a credit report.
Kevin Bangston, who leads Daimler’s financial services arm in North America, described the connected ecosystem built around the manufacturer’s Detroit Connect system and was candid that the company uses it for a wide range of purposes. On the service side, the data helps decode whether a truck has a problem that can safely wait until the next scheduled maintenance or whether something needs immediate attention, which ties directly into how warranty claims get prioritized and handled. That alone changes the economics of uptime, because catching the difference between a wait-and-fix and a fix-now can save a breakdown on the road.
But the more consequential uses are financial. Bangston acknowledged that in the cases where loans default, the connected data helps the company locate its trucks, and because it knows where the trucks are, it is actually reducing its losses. Read that plainly. The same system that tells you your truck needs service also tells your lender where to find it if you stop paying. That is not sinister on its face, it is how a modern secured lender manages risk, but it is a reminder that the data flows both ways.
Connected Insurance And The Geico Pilot
The clearest example of data becoming your rate is insurance. Daimler announced a connected insurance program with Geico, and Bangston said it was tailored primarily for small fleets rather than mega fleets, with the company looking at how to extend a similar approach to mid-sized and large operations in another format down the road.
The idea behind connected insurance is that precise, real-world data about how a truck is actually operated and where it is can be used to price coverage more accurately than traditional broad-brush underwriting. For a safe, well-run small operation, that is potentially good news, because it opens a path to being priced on your actual behavior rather than lumped in with everyone in your category. The flip side is the obvious one. If data can reward the careful operator, it can also flag the one whose trucks are driven hard, and the same transparency that lowers one carrier’s premium can raise another’s. The reporter’s instinct to call it a new credit score was not far off, because that is exactly how a score works, it turns your behavior into a number that other people price off of.
Faster Money, Built On Data And AI
The data story runs straight into financing, and here the news is mostly good for carriers. Stephan Unger, chairman of Daimler Truck Financial Services, and Bangston both described how artificial intelligence and analytics are compressing the time it takes to make a credit decision from days down to hours. For a carrier waiting on approval to put a truck to work, that speed is real value, and Unger tied it directly back to customer benefit, noting that faster, more efficient decisioning can also flow through to better terms.
Behind the scenes, Daimler is also using advanced analytics on its own portfolio, learning from the pain of the multi-year freight recession to build something more resilient. Bangston described using smart analytics to figure out how to construct a portfolio that performs better in the next downturn and to target where the company should be acquiring business. The company even noted that its head of operations is the driving force behind its AI activity in North America. What this means for you is that the same data-and-analytics machine that speeds up your approval is also constantly assessing which kinds of carriers and segments represent good risk, which quietly shapes who gets the easiest access to financing and on what terms.
The Two Sides Every Carrier Should Weigh
So is this good or bad for a small carrier? Honestly, both, and pretending otherwise would not serve you.
On the upside, connected data can lower your insurance if you run clean, speed up your financing, catch mechanical problems before they strand you, and help you prove you are a professional operation worth doing business with. For a careful operator, data is a chance to be judged on your actual record rather than a stereotype about small fleets.
On the other side, the same data gives lenders and insurers a level of visibility into your operation they never had before, from how your trucks are driven to where they sit to when you are struggling. It can locate your equipment if you fall behind, and it can feed decisions about your rates and your terms that you do not fully see. The reporter who asked whether this is his new credit score was pointing at a genuine shift in power, because a score is something others control and price you on. The practical response is not to reject the technology, which is becoming unavoidable, but to understand that your telematics is now part of your financial reputation, to run your operation knowing it is being measured, and to ask pointed questions about what data is collected, who sees it, and how it affects your rate before you sign up for connected programs.
Why It Matters
The data a fleet’s trucks generate has quietly crossed the line from operational tool to financial instrument, now feeding insurance pricing, credit decisions that have compressed from days to hours, warranty triage, and even asset recovery on defaulted loans. For fleet and finance leaders, that means the same transparency that can lower premiums for a well-run operation and speed access to capital also hands insurers and lenders a level of visibility into the business they never had, so the strategic question is no longer whether to connect but how to govern that data, understand how it shapes rates and terms, and treat it as the reputational asset and exposure it has become.
This article is based on a panel discussion with Daimler Truck and Daimler Truck Financial Services leadership at the DTFS North American headquarters in Charlotte, North Carolina, featuring Stephan Unger, chairman of Daimler Truck Financial Services, and Kevin Bangston, president and CEO of Daimler Truck Financial Services USA LLC. Program details and statements are as presented by the executives.

It was hard not to read the quarterly letter to shareholders by Aaron Graft, the CEO of Triumph Financial, and not get a sense that he was taking the first few steps into a victory lap.
Triumph’s message to investors for years has been consistent, and it has been amplified every three months in Graft’s multi-page letter to shareholders, unique among CEOs.
That message has been that Triumph Financial (NYSE: TFIN) , while still being a bank at its most basic definition, was building an infrastructure to become the supplier of a vast array of financial support services to the trucking community, all the way down to independent owner operators.
Factoring? Got it, since it’s essentially the original Triumph Financial business. Payments? Ever since Triumph Financial bought HubTran in 2021, it has been building its Payments system to process invoices. Intelligence? It bought Green Sheets last year. How about what amounts to a digital wallet for drivers and small fleets? It launched LoadPay in 2024 for that purpose.
While this was going on, it hasn’t been an easy ride for investors. Triumph Financial stock is down about 43.5% over the last five years.
But the data released in the company’s third quarter earnings report featured numbers that were almost universally positive and suggested those years of investment–which pinched profitability–are starting to pay off.
More importantly are the company’s North Star Metrics , which Triumph Financial set two quarters ago.
Those North Star metrics in the third quarter broke down as follows:
Transportation Revenue Growth: Long-term target is above 15% growth, third quarter was 37.8%. About a third of it is organic, so it is not just being pushed higher on the back of a stronger freight market and higher diesel prices.
Factoring operating margin : Long-term target is above 40%, third quarter was 43%.
Payments EBITDA, exclusive of the LoadPay wallet offering: More than 50%, 39% in the third quarter after being 34% in the second quarter.
Intelligence Gross Margin: Above 85%, but Graft said in his letter that metric will be dropped from its North Star goals. Intelligence revenue was a mere $2.4 million, down slightly sequentially.
“We told investors we would invest through the freight cycle , and we did exactly that,” Graft wrote in his letter. “ Not everyone agreed with the strategy , but we were true to our word.”
Triumph will now look to “translate that potential into earnings performance consistent with our historical results and beyond,” Graft wrote. “Doing so will demonstrate the returns on the investments we have made.”
Triumph Financial’s revenues have been impacted since the start of the Iran war by higher diesel prices. Even if the linehaul portion of a freight invoice stays flat, if the price of diesel rises, that number goes into the invoice it factors or processes (or both), which as Graft conceded in his letter has always led to the question: “How sensitive (is) our average invoice prices…to the cost of diesel?”
Graft’s answer was complicated and simple at the same time: it depends. Factors that would go into answering that question can vary widely among customers, including such things as the carrier’s fuel surcharge formula.
But Graft did seek to answer the question. Year-on-year, he said, dry van revenue is up 40% but diesel costs, as measured at the pump (as opposed to trucker fuel discounts) have risen by 67% during that time. Driver costs have risen, with Graft putting a figure of 70 cents/mile on current levels.
Throw in insurance, interest costs and equipment, and Graft laid out an inflationary landscape.
We don't know what % of invoices processed at $TFIN are #diesel costs, so it's not easy to draw a conclusion from 3Q earnings that avg size of invoices rose 2.3% while diesel costs rose 3.9%. Also: an avg figure for diesel covers up crazy volatility. Low to high was almost $2. pic.twitter.com/8pMFJab4NP — John Kingston (@JohnHKingston) October 21, 2026
“As a result, the revenue per mile a trucker must generate and thus the average invoice size is almost certainly going to be double-digit percentages above historical norms until market forces change,” he wrote.
But Graft ultimately did provide a benchmark on what the market means for the company. For every $100 upward move in the average invoice price, he wrote, “Triumph should generate roughly $12 million in incremental annual revenue, $8.5 million in pretax earnings and 27 cents in earnings per share,” he said.
But he added: “The inverse is also true when invoice sizes decline.”
While Factoring in recent years might have been considered the less sexy part of the Triumph business, with so much focus on the Payment sector, Graft used the third quarter letter to promote that sector.
He disclosed several pieces of data. Graft said according to Triumph’s data, there are more than 90,000 “factored carriers” in the U.S. Triumph services about 8,000 of them, growing at the rate of 78 net new clients per month.
He also said costs to service an invoice have dropped by about 20% in the last year.
But Graft said Factoring’s importance at Triumph has grown for other reasons besides the bottom line.
Like the quarterly earnings at $CHRW , that of $TFIN has data that shows increased productivity. Triumph's Factoring business is processing more invoices with fewer people, though the declines are not as stark as seen at C.H. Robinson. (Admittedly different businesses). pic.twitter.com/ZYhHd0u4F6 — John Kingston (@JohnHKingston) October 21, 2026
“Factoring remains both an attractive financial business and the principal carrier-acquisition gateway into the Triumph value chain,” Graft wrote. “When we win a factoring relationship, we have an opportunity to serve that carrier through LoadPay, equipment finance, insurance, fuel, and Intelligence. The economic value of Factoring therefore extends beyond the margin earned on an individual receivable. That broader relationship is one reason renewed growth in this business remains a strategic priority.”
Among other data points and observations in Graft’s letter:
Graft did not mention the decision in Montgomery vs. Caribe Transport II . But it was hard not to think of it when he wrote: “The scarce resource in freight today is not trucks. It is trusted, deployable capacity, because a truck that cannot be verified and deployed with confidence is not defensible, and thus, is not truly usable capacity. Freight is moving from a market defined by abundant capacity to one defined by defensible capacity.”
EBITDA in the Payments sector had been negative for many quarters. Progress was often measured in just how much negative EBITDA had been reduced, though Payments has been a positive EBITDA margin for more than a year. “The Payments business has graduated from logo acquisition to revenue growth to EBITDA margin expansion and, finally, is becoming a driver of earnings,” Graft said. “As a result, we will provide more commentary on operating income in future letters alongside insights on revenue growth and EBITDA margin. Over the next several quarters, we expect operating income to continue to grow through a balanced combination of organic revenue growth and cost savings with less contribution from repricing.” The Payments EBITDA whether it was 30.8% for the full Payments group or the group’s margin excluding LoadPay of 39%, was the highest in the company’s history.

Global logistics provider DSV has opened a new $90 million, 853,000-square-foot logistics facility in Laredo, Texas, expanding its capacity to handle freight moving between the U.S. and Mexico .
The facility consolidates warehousing, transportation, customs brokerage, inventory management and distribution services under one roof, the company announced Wednesday.
The investment is part of DSV’s broader strategy to strengthen its North American cross-border logistics network , which also includes a recently opened office in McAllen, Texas .
“Our Laredo facility is a milestone in DSV’s strategy to lead with innovation and scale,” Josh Summers, CEO of Contract Logistics, North America, said in a news release . “We’re committed to helping our customers grow by providing smarter, more agile logistics solutions.”
The new multi-client complex is located along Interstate 35 in Laredo, one of the nation’s busiest gateways for commercial trade with Mexico.
According to FreightWaves SONAR, shippers currently hold solid negotiating leverage with carriers in Laredo. As of Oct. 21, the Outbound Tender Rejection Index (STRI) has dropped from 8.15% a month ago to 5.10%
In Laredo, Texas, carriers are facing a loosening environment with outbound tender rejections (STRI.LRD) falling to 5.10%, giving shippers the upper hand. To learn more about FreightWaves SONAR, click here .
DSV broke ground on the new project in Laredo in July 2025 at a 49-acre site within Majestic Realty’s Port Grande Logistics Park, a 2,000-acre industrial development.
The facility supports a range of logistics operations, including cross-docking, e-commerce fulfillment, inventory management, distribution and cross-border transportation.
It also offers bonded warehousing and Foreign-Trade Zone storage options, along with northbound U.S. customs services and on-site Mexican customs processing.
Those capabilities are designed to help shippers reduce delays, streamline customs clearance and improve freight visibility when moving goods between the two countries.
The facilities in Laredo and McAllen complement DSV’s existing border operations in Brownsville, El Paso and Los Indios, Texas, as well as San Diego, California.
The Laredo operation is part of DSV’s global logistics network, which employs approximately 150,000 people in more than 90 countries.
Why it matters: DSV’s investments in Laredo and McAllen, Texas, adds integrated freight handling and customs capabilities at one of North America’s busiest trade gateways.

source_document.body:
Tesla now says unsupervised “Full Self-Driving” in customer-owned cars will arrive in Q2 2027. It’s the latest date on a promise Elon Musk has been making to FSD buyers for the better part of a decade.
But there’s a catch. On Tesla’s Q3 2026 earnings call today, AI chief Ashok Elluswamy described it as owners adding their own vehicles to Tesla’s managed Robotaxi fleet, not owners getting a car that drives them anywhere they want to go.
The question shareholders actually asked
“When can we anticipate FSD unsupervised in customer cars?” was one of the top retail shareholder questions submitted for the call, backed by about 1.1 million shares, as we noted in our Tesla Q3 2026 earnings preview .
Elluswamy’s answer was Q2 2027. And the way he framed it, step one isn’t a software update that lets you climb into the back of your Model Y and sleep while it drives you to your destination – what Elon Musk sold to customers since 2016. It’s Tesla letting owners put their cars into its own Robotaxi network, where Tesla runs the operation.

So an owner’s car would only drive itself unsupervised where Tesla’s Robotaxi already operates.
Those zones are small
Tesla’s Robotaxi service runs in six US metros right now, and most of the service areas cover small slices of those cities. When Tesla mapped its Miami Robotaxi zone , it covered mostly West Miami and a strip toward Doral and Sweetwater. Orlando and Tampa launched in July with similarly small geofences.
Inside those zones, the service sticks to low-speed routes, largely stays off highways, and avoids the harder parts of town. In the Bay Area, it isn’t unsupervised at all. California rules still require a safety driver in every car because Tesla doesn’t want to release data to the California DMV, which it has to do beyond a level 2 autonomous system.
The fleet is small too. Tesla says Robotaxi reached nearly 2 million cumulative unsupervised miles by the end of Q3, a month after Cybercab joined the Austin fleet, according to Tesla’s Q3 2026 results . Third-party tracking this spring showed the number of fully driverless Teslas on the road in the dozens, nowhere near the hundreds of thousands Musk had talked about. Waymo, meanwhile, was already in both Orlando and Tampa before Tesla showed up, and it has over 3 million miles.
The promise vs. the product
That’s not what Tesla sold. For years, the pitch to FSD buyers was a car that would eventually drive itself anywhere through a software update.
Musk told investors in July 2025 that unsupervised FSD would be available “for unsupervised personal use by the end of this year in certain geographies.” A year earlier, he said he’d be “surprised” if Tesla didn’t have unsupervised self-driving the following year . And HW3 owners who bought FSD have already been told their computers can’t run unsupervised FSD at all, with no clear upgrade plan.
Now the target is Q2 2027, and the product is narrower: your car joins Tesla’s fleet, in Tesla’s zones, on Tesla’s terms.
Electrek’s Take
If you can believe it. Believing a Tesla FSD timeline is a fool’s errand at this point, and I don’t see any reason to treat Q2 2027 differently from every other date Tesla has given since 2019.
But even if it happens on time, look at what’s actually being promised. This moves the goalpost from “your car drives you anywhere while you sleep” to “your car can work as a Robotaxi inside a small geofence that Tesla controls.” No highway road trips. No driving you home from the airport across town. No unsupervised commute unless you happen to live and work inside one of the zones.
It’s the goalpost moving of all goalpost moving. If one thing was clear from the call, Tesla has no idea when it will actually happen. They are just guessing. Ashok again reiterated that safety is the bottleneck, which is why Tesla limits itself to low-speed roads and harder environments. He guesses that those safety issues will be fixed by next year, but he doesn’t know.

source_document.body:
Fuel prices jumped 17 spots to become the trucking industry’s biggest concern in 2026, according to the American Transportation Research Institute ’s annual Top Industry Issues report . Lawsuit reform ranked second, while concerns about federal carrier safety scores climbed to third.
What’s Related
The economy , which topped the list for three consecutive years, fell to sixth. Driver shortages and retention returned to the top 10, and artificial intelligence moved up as respondents weighed its uses against risks to jobs , security and cargo theft.
ATRI gathered responses from more than 3,000 trucking industry participants, who selected and ranked their three biggest concerns. Here are the top 10 issues, in order.
1. Fuel Prices
Fuel costs topped the list for the first time since 2022, with 30% of respondents placing them among their three biggest concerns. ATRI noted that rising diesel prices immediately pressured fleet budgets, particularly for smaller carriers. The leading proposed response was federal action to stabilize fuel supplies and limit price increases.
2. Lawsuit Abuse Reform
Lawsuit reform remained second overall and became the top concern among motor carrier respondents. ATRI pointed to the financial pressure from large verdicts and settlements and their impact on insurance costs. Respondents favored state limits on certain damages, changes to medical expense claims, and greater disclosure of outside funding for lawsuits.
RELATED STORIES: Ranking the Top 50 Trucking Companies in the U.S. for 2025 | 2024 Rankings
3. Compliance Safety Accountability
Concerns about the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration’s Compliance Safety Accountability program rose three spots to their highest ranking since 2015. The program uses inspection and crash data to assess carrier safety. Respondents’ leading priority was addressing differences in state and local enforcement that can affect scores based on where fleets travel.
4. Insurance Cost and Availability
Insurance slipped one position but remained a major expense concern. ATRI cited research showing carrier liability premiums rose 18.2% from 2021 through 2024, while truck crash involvement declined 2.6%. Respondents favored developing a way for fleets investing in proven safety technology to receive upfront premium reductions.
5. Driver Shortage
Driver shortages returned to the top 10 after falling off the list in 2025. ATRI said carriers had reduced driver counts during the freight downturn, leaving concerns about hiring as demand begins to improve. Proposed responses included promoting trucking careers and creating paths for younger workers to enter the industry before becoming drivers.
6. Economy
The economy fell from first to sixth, although the report described continued pressure from weak profits and rising expenses. ATRI’s latest trucking cost research put non-fuel costs at a record $1.854 per mile. Respondents wanted more research into how trucking expenses and tariffs affect equipment purchases, freight demand, and consumer prices.
7. Artificial Intelligence in Trucking
AI climbed three positions after entering the top 10 last year. The report highlighted uses such as driver coaching and predicting maintenance needs, alongside concerns about job displacement and increasingly sophisticated cargo theft. Respondents’ top recommendation was research into AI’s practical uses and its positive and negative effects on trucking jobs.
8. Diesel Emissions Regulations
Diesel emissions rules ranked eighth, reflecting concerns about truck prices, maintenance and the introduction of new emissions equipment. Respondents prioritized measuring compliance costs and allowing more flexibility in implementing stricter standards. The report also called for tracking how new emissions systems perform and hold up in everyday service.
9. Driver Compensation
Driver pay dropped four spots overall but remained the third-biggest concern among truck drivers and the top issue for company drivers. Respondents favored studying how different pay arrangements, including hourly, mileage and per-load pay, affect satisfaction, productivity and retention. Another priority was evaluating safety, fuel economy and retention bonuses.
10. Driver Retention
Keeping drivers returned to the overall top 10 for the first time since 2023. Respondents wanted a better understanding of why drivers leave and what low-turnover fleets do differently. ATRI cited research linking higher pay and shorter waits at customer facilities with lower driver turnover.

Amazon plans to hire more than 300,000 people across the United States for the holiday season , increasing its hiring target by about 20% from last year as it prepares for the busiest stretch of the shipping calendar.
What’s Related
The company said the openings include seasonal, part-time and full-time positions. The hiring covers the fulfillment and transportation work that gets customer orders picked , packed, sorted and delivered during the holiday rush.
Amazon sought 250,000 workers during last year’s holiday season. This year’s target adds more than 50,000 positions to that total, with new openings scheduled to be posted weekly from October through December.
Seasonal employees will earn an average of $20 an hour. Amazon also announced expanded health coverage for eligible seasonal workers, although that change will begin January 1, 2027.

Amazon to invest $1.5 billion on higher pay
The hiring announcement follows Amazon’s September commitment to spend more than $1.5 billion on higher pay for its U.S. fulfillment and transportation employees. That included a $1 hourly increase for eligible workers.
Full-time employees in those roles now start at a minimum of $20 an hour, with average hourly pay reaching nearly $24. Amazon puts average total compensation above $32 an hour when benefits are included.
The company also introduced employee grocery discounts this month. Those include 10% off eligible online grocery and everyday essentials purchases and 20% off purchases at Whole Foods Market stores.

source_document.body:
Photo: Rondo
Rio Tinto wants to put Australia’s cheap midday electricity to work at its Yarwun alumina refinery – by storing it in hot bricks and using that heat battery to make steam after the sun sets.
The global mining giant and California-based Rondo Energy have started engineering and design work on a huge heat battery near Gladstone, Queensland. Rondo calls it Australia’s largest planned thermal energy storage project and says it would be a first for the alumina industry.
Alumina is a hard white powder made of aluminum and oxygen that’s used to make aluminum metal, sandpaper, and strong ceramics. Globally, aluminum sector refining accounts for roughly 175 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent annually.
It’s still at the study stage, but the potential payoff is substantial. Rio Tinto estimates the battery could supply around 5% of Yarwun’s steam needs and cut the refinery’s direct emissions by about 67,000 metric tons of carbon dioxide annually. It would replace some of the coal and natural gas used to generate steam.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Rondo’s heat battery uses electricity to heat refractory bricks, which can withstand high temperatures. The bricks hold that energy as heat, which is then used to produce steam for the refinery’s existing steam network.
That matters because industrial heat demand doesn’t stop when solar production drops. Rondo’s heat battery charges during hours when electricity is cheap and plentiful, then delivers heat continuously so factories can keep running.
The proposed Yarwun system would have 360 megawatt-hours (MWh) of thermal storage and deliver up to 30 megawatts MW of heat. The Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA) lists its electrical charging capacity at 78 MW, allowing it to take in electricity faster than it releases the stored energy as heat.
For the refinery, another attraction is that the battery would feed into equipment it already uses. The study will assess whether that integration can deliver reliable high-pressure steam at a cost that makes sense.
“This project shows how Australia’s abundant energy can become a competitive advantage for industry,” said Dr. Kira Rundel, Rondo’s head of Australia. “Heat batteries allow manufacturers to use low-cost electricity to produce the reliable, round-the-clock heat their operations need.”
ARENA is providing an initial A$3.6 million for the engineering and design study. If the project moves ahead, the agency will provide up to A$38 million for deployment. There’s also a further A$33.3 million in contingency support.
Rio Tinto will match ARENA’s A$3.6 million study contribution. The company says its total investment over the project’s life is expected to exceed ARENA’s funding if deployment goes ahead.
“Reducing emissions from alumina refining is complex, particularly when it comes to generating the high-pressure steam needed for our operations,” said Rio Tinto Pacific Operations managing director Armando Torres.
“This study will help us determine whether thermal energy storage can provide a technically and economically viable alternative to fossil fuels for part of Yarwun’s steam requirements.”
The feasibility study is expected to take about 12 months.

source_document.body:
DoorDash’s move into retail returns raises a practical question: Will shoppers pay $7.99 to skip a trip to drop off a package? In this Q&A, Andrew Schmid , Chief Product Officer at Route and a former Nike retail executive, discusses what makes doorstep returns worth the price, what retailers need to handle behind the scenes, and how to measure whether the service is working.
What’s Related
Supply Chain 24/7: What stands out to you about DoorDash’s new retail returns service?
Andrew Schmid: What stands out to me is that DoorDash is moving further into a part of retail that has historically been pretty fragmented. Returns are a huge expense for retailers, and getting a product from someone's doorstep back into the supply chain is only one piece of that. I think we'll see more delivery and logistics companies trying to own more of the customer experience, especially as competition heats up. The new question, though, is whether that added convenience creates enough value for shoppers and retailers to justify yet another cost in the returns process.
SC247: Will shoppers pay $7.99 for a return pickup?
Schmid: I think some shoppers absolutely will, but it depends on what they're returning and how much hassle the service saves them. If I'm returning a $200 pair of shoes and don't have time to get to a drop-off location, $7.99 might feel pretty reasonable. But for a $25 item, that's a much harder sell, especially when every dollar counts for consumers right now. Retailers also have to decide whether shoppers should pay for it, the brand should fund it or it should be a benefit for their most loyal customers.
SC247: What needs to happen behind the scenes between the pickup and the customer getting a refund?
Schmid: There's a lot more happening behind the scenes than most shoppers realize. The retailer needs to know the item was picked up, track it through the return process, determine when to issue a refund and decide what happens to that inventory once it comes back. When a refund is late, the shopper isn’t weighing whether the warehouse scan failed or the returns platform never got the update. They just want their money back. That requires the systems handling pickups, returns and refunds to all communicate with each other.
Andrew Schmid
SC247: What should retailers have in place before offering a service like this?
Schmid: I'd start by looking at how well your existing returns process works before adding another pickup option. A common challenge is that tracking, customer support, returns and exchanges often live in separate systems that aren’t connected. Adding DoorDash to that process creates another handoff, so retailers need to make sure pickup confirmations, return statuses and refund information actually get where they need to go. I'd want a clear understanding of which customers would use the service and whether the retailer can support the additional volume without creating more problems for its operations team. There’s also an unanswered question about cost: Does the shopper or the brand eat it?
SC247: Where do you see the highest costs, and what would it take to make this profitable?
Schmid: Having spent years working in retail operations, I can tell you the return label is only a fraction of the expense. You've got transportation , receiving, inspecting the product and then deciding whether it goes back into inventory, gets discounted or can't be resold at all. Each step adds another cost. Adding doorstep pickup creates another cost before the product even enters that process, so the economics have to make sense. I'd be looking at whether DoorDash can keep pickup costs down by combining returns with existing delivery routes and whether the service actually reduces costs elsewhere in the process. If it just makes an already expensive return more expensive, retailers will find it hard to sustain.
SC247: How could faster return pickups help retailers get products back on shelves and ready to sell again?
Schmid: Speed matters, especially for seasonal products or inventory that's only valuable for a short window. But getting an item off someone's doorstep faster doesn't necessarily mean it's available to sell again any sooner. It still needs to move through receiving, inspection and whatever process the retailer uses to get it back into inventory. A return physically received but never recorded is exactly the kind of operational gap that can erase the benefit of a faster pickup. Retailers need to look at how long the entire process takes, from the moment a shopper requests a return to when that product is actually available for someone else to buy.
SC247: How does adding returns change DoorDash’s competition with Uber and other delivery services?
Schmid: I think we're heading into a pretty interesting period of competition and consolidation across logistics. DoorDash and Uber have already built networks designed to move things quickly, and returns give them another opportunity to put that infrastructure to work. We're seeing a similar push toward consolidation with C.H. Robinson 's acquisition of RXO, as companies look for ways to offer more supply chain services. My question is how much of that expansion retailers actually need and whether the economics work. Amazon has the scale and logistics infrastructure to absorb rising fulfillment and delivery costs, but most retailers don't have that luxury.
SC247: For an e-commerce brand considering doorstep returns, what should it measure to decide whether the service is working?
Schmid: I'd want to understand how many shoppers are actually choosing doorstep pickup and what it's costing the retailer for each completed return. Then I'd look at whether products are getting back into sellable inventory faster, whether refund timelines are improving and whether customer service teams are seeing fewer questions about returns. Return and exchange rates, customer support inquiries, refund timelines and repeat purchase behavior give a much more complete picture of how the experience is working. Ultimately, retailers need to understand whether the convenience is valuable enough to customers to justify the cost, and whether it's helping them grow their business .
Andrew Schmid is Chief Product Officer at Route .

Tesla said today it will sell Cybercab to consumers by the end of this year, raising questions of what end users would do with a vehicle with no steering wheel and no self-driving software.
During Tesla’s Q3 conference call today , a question was asked about when Tesla will deliver unsupervised FSD to customer cars.
That question was answered slightly differently than usual. Instead of the standard “end of next year” that we’ve heard every year for a decade , Tesla changed the answer to: “middle of next year.” In order words, Q2 2027.
So, alright, that’s when Tesla says its cars will be able to drive themselves with nobody paying any attention. Great. It would be quite a big step from their current level 2 system to a level 4 or 5 system, which are the only categories that could be deemed as “unsupervised” as level 3 still includes a driver in the driver’s seat who needs to be ready to take control at any time.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
But then, in the same question, Tesla made another prediction. VP of Engineering Lars Moravy said that Cybercab will be in customer hands by the end of this year – which means within the next two months. Here’s the answer:
In short we’re trying to get Cybercabs to customers by the end of this year in 2026, obviously we’re producing a lot in Texas but all of those are going to our own internal Robotaxi fleet, and as Tesla grows we’ll mainly deliver fully designed autonomous vehicles to our customers and Cybercab will be the first. And so as we start small this year and we learn about all the things Ashok mentioned about delivery and ownership and fleet management and autonomous vehicles in customer hands, we’ll continue to scale that.
Musk then added on to the answer, highlighting that Cybercabs would mostly be Tesla-owned transport-as-a-service vehicles, which somewhat contradicts Tesla’s call for Cybercab fleet buyers which it put out the same day as its Cybercab launch event .
But did you notice anything? Moravy said that Cybercabs would be in customer hands – that is, not Tesla’s hands – by the end of 2026. And Ashok, in his answer which we reported on here, said unsupervised FSD would be in customer hands in Q2 2027 (if that’s to be believed).
This would leave a half-year where these Cybercabs, which are intended to come with no steering wheel or pedals, are completely inoperable. You couldn’t even push them into your driveway, because you’d have no steering wheel to help you do so.
Unless, of course, these Cybercabs get delivered with steering wheels – which most of the ones in the wild have these days anyway . And if they did, then why not just call it a Model 2 and sell it to people for $25k, like you should have done in the first place ?
Either that, or the vehicles will be limited to the same areas that Cybercabs are already limited to. Despite Musk predicting that Robotaxis would cover half the US population by the end of last year , it is currently available only in small portions of 6 cities in 2 states .

Knight-Swift Transportation beat third-quarter expectations Wednesday after the market closed.
Knight-Swift ( NYSE: KNX ) reported adjusted earnings per share of 83 cents, 51 cents higher than the year-ago quarter and 7 cents better than the consensus estimate. ( Management’s EPS guidance range was 71 to 77 cents.)
Revenue of $2.2 billion was up 14% y/y (up 8% y/y excluding fuel surcharges) and slightly ahead of analysts’ expectations for $2.17 billion.
“Similar to our outlook last quarter, we expect momentum across our businesses to keep building as rates continue to be reset, as we maintain our cost and operational initiatives, and as we anticipate more seasonal spot and project opportunities than we have seen in recent years,” said Knight-Swift CEO Adam Miller in a news release.
The truckload unit saw a 6.5% y/y revenue increase (ex-fuel) as an 11% increase in revenue per tractor was only partially offset by a 4% decline in average tractors in service. Loaded miles per tractor were up 1% y/y, an eighth consecutive increase. Deadhead was down 170 basis points y/y to 12.1%. Revenue per loaded mile (ex-fuel) increased 10% y/y. The metric was up by a mid-teen percentage in its over-the-road service.
The TL unit posted an 89.2% adjusted operating ratio, 700 bps better y/y and in line with the midpoint of management’s guidance range. U.S. Xpress, which was acquired in 2023 , operated at a low-90% adjusted OR in the quarter while Knight-Swift’s legacy brands operated at 88%.
Table: Knight-Swift’s key performance indicators
Less-than-truckload revenue was up less than 1% y/y (ex-fuel). Tonnage increased 3% while revenue per hundredweight (ex-fuel) dipped 1%. Increases in weight per shipment (+5%) and length of haul (+6%) had mostly offsetting impacts on yield in the quarter. Revenue per shipment (ex-fuel) increased 4%. Contractual renewals were up by a mid-single-digit percentage.
The LTL unit booked a 91.4% adjusted OR, 80 bps worse y/y.
Knight-Swift issued fourth-quarter adjusted EPS guidance of 78 to 84 cents, which bracketed the 82-cent consensus estimate at the time of the print.
The third-quarter adjusted EPS number benefitted y/y from a $22-million reduction in net interest expense (10 cents per share), a lower tax rate (5 cents per share) and a slight increase in gains on equipment sales (1 cent per share). However, the other income line was down $3.5 million y/y (2 cents per share).
Shares of KNX were up 4.4% in after-hours trading on Wednesday.
The company will host a call at 5:30 p.m. EDT on Wednesday to discuss third-quarter results.
Why it matters? Knight-Swift is the nation’s largest asset-based TL carrier and serves as a bellwether for market trends. The company’s third-quarter results highlight that the market has transitioned from a cyclical downturn to a structural recovery.

1966 Chevrolet Corvette With 570 Miles on the Clock Rocks Black-on-Black and a Small-Block V8
18 photos
Photo: Bring a Trailer
This C2 Chevrolet Corvette rocks a black-on-black color scheme, a small-block V8, a manual gearbox, and only 570 miles on the clock. The car was restored back in 2010, but the original engine and transmission have stood their ground. Now, the C2 Corvette is looking for a new home.
Just 570 miles or 917 kilometers in 16 years. This is how far this 1966 Chevrolet Corvette has traveled since it was restored in 2010. That sort of mileage makes it the ultimate garage queen, without a doubt.
Three years after the restoration was completed, the car changed hands, and it is still with that owner. However, it won't be for long, because the owner listed it for sale. And the C2 Corvette seems to check all the right boxes.
It is powered by a rebuilt 327-cubic-inch V8, which was the highest-output small-block engine available in 1966, but was completely outperformed by the big-block 427-cubic-inch V8, which made its debut with the 1966 model year.
Photo: Bring a Trailer The 427-cubic-inch V8 engine produced either 390 horsepower or 425 horsepower in its top form. That was, however, the official rating. The engine was known to push out roughly 25 horsepower more. General Motors deliberately downgraded the advertised number on paper just before launch to appease insurance companies.
In the meantime, the 327 had no such issues. Although the 427 big-blocks dominated straight-line acceleration, many enthusiasts preferred the L79 small-block. The lighter 327 engine kept the Corvette's weight balanced, meaning L79-powered cars handled backroads and sharp corners much better than the nose-heavy 427 variants.
The 327 came in two flavors: as an L75 with 300 horsepower (304 metric horsepower) and as an L79 with 350 horsepower (355 metric horsepower). According to the listing, the L79 with a four-barrel carburetor is the setup that gets this car moving. Before the engine got rebuilt, it came with the aforementioned 350 horsepower and 360 pound-feet (488 Newton meters) of torque.
Photo: Bring a Trailer The car could rocket from zero to hero (0 to 60 mph or 0 to 97 kph) in 5.4 seconds and max out at 135 mph (217 kph). The four-speed manual transmission puts the power down through the rear wheels in typical Corvette manner. There is no info about how much the small block makes after it was rebuilt, but what we do know is that a dual exhaust system roars out all the drama of the V8.
Finished in black over black and featuring flip-up headlights and a black convertible top, the C2 with its fiberglass body rides on turbine-style aluminum wheels, shod in gold-line BFGoodrich Radial tires. Back in 1966, this car rolled off the production line wearing silver, but that changed in 2010. The 'Vette comes with chrome bumpers and a driver-side mirror.
The car is equipped with power steering, while power-assisted four-wheel discs provide the stopping power. The C2 Corvette was the first of its kind to feature a fully independent suspension with upper and lower control arms up front and a three-link setup with a transverse leaf spring out back.
Photo: Bring a Trailer The cabin hosts two bucket seats upholstered in black leather and sporting lap belts, along with color-coordinated door panels and carpets. Air conditioning makes traveling comfortable regardless of the weather, while an AM/FM radio provides the soundtrack on board.
The three-spoke steering wheel frames a speedometer scaled up to 160 mph (258 kph), sitting in the company of the tachometer and auxiliary gauges for fuel level, amperage, oil pressure, and water temperature. The five-digit odometer reads 570 miles. However, the true mileage of the Corvette remains unknown.
The C2 convertible is offered on dealer consignment with a clean Illinois title. The seller highlights that it was not involved in any accidents that he knows of. So, it is now in search of a new home. With five days to go, the highest bid sits at $55,000.
Back in 1966, a C2 Chevrolet Corvette with the high-performance L79 used to start at around $4,400 before options or taxes. The L79 engine cost an extra $105.35 back in the day. To get the L79, buyers also had to opt for the Muncie four-speed manual transmission, adding another $184.35 to the final price.
Photo: Bring a Trailer Combined with delivery fees and a few common options, most L79 Corvettes walked out the door in 1966 for roughly $4,800. Adjusted for inflation, that equates to roughly $47,000 today, when the most affordable Corvette starts at $71,300.
Nowadays, such cars go for an average of $85,661, as reported by classic.com. However, models that underwent restoration but retain the original driveline, like this car does, often command over $90,000. Convertibles generally command a slight pricing premium over standard coupes.
And that is despite the fact that 1966 was the highest-selling year of the entire C2 generation, with 27,720 units sold, so you can uncheck the exclusivity box.

Buried in a press release titled, “Even more colours and even greater convenience for the Cayenne Electric” was news that Porsche, for the first time, would be offering electrically wireless inductive charging on its impressively powerful Cayenne Electric SUV.
UPDATE 21OCT2026 : now, there’s a video .
In a new explainer video released today, Porsche explains how its engineers developed inductive charging for the Cayenne Electric, from the transfer of power across an air gap to detecting foreign objects, guiding the car into position, and testing the system in real-world conditions without microwaving the family pet.
You can click the “play” button, at top, and read the original press release that came out a few weeks ago, below. Enjoy!
Advertisement - scroll for more content
With the launch of Porsche Wireless Charging in its latest Cayenne Electric SUV, Porsche is introducing a particularly convenient form of EV charging that makes living with its most powerful car EVER even simpler than before : instead of connecting a cable, Cayenne drivers just have to park their portly P-car over a strategically placed pad, and the charging process then begins automatically .
The Porsche Wireless Charging system pairs a charging pad on the underside of the Cayenne with a ground pad installed in the customer’s parking space. Porsche calls the latter “weatherproof” for outdoor installation, and claims a charging rate of up to 11 kW and with an efficiency of about 90% for easy overnight charging.
Integrated safety mechanisms like motion sensors and cat foreign object detection are baked in to avoid microwaving the cat ensure safe operation , designed to stop the charging process automatically if, “a living creature comes close to the vehicle or the ground pad or if a metallic object lies on the latter and heats up.”
Porsche Wireless Charging is being rolled out globally in stages, and is available to order now in Germany and other European markets.
